clue.text: Celebrate birth and baptism at same time?

definitions.text: Celebrate birth and baptism at same time?

blocks.note: surface reading: marking a new arrival, the way a family toasts a newborn
setter's reading: at a christening water is poured over the infant's head, so the drinking idiom also describes the rite literally

explanation.surface: A thrifty family wonders whether the birth party and the christening could be rolled into one.
explanation.walkthrough: The British idiom for celebrating a birth with a drink describes, read literally, exactly what a priest does at baptism, so one phrase covers both occasions.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means toasting a newborn with drinks, while the literal sense is the sprinkling of water during christening.

clue.text: Revolting peasant meeting impudent girl in cave!

indicators.note: meeting means coming together, so the two people are joined end to end

blocks.note: Wat Tyler led the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381
a chit is a cheeky young girl

explanation.surface: A rebellious peasant meets a cheeky girl in a cave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cave' is not a hollow: it is Latin for 'beware', schoolboy slang shouted when a teacher approached (pronounced KAY-vee).
explanation.definitionFit: Both are warnings telling someone to be careful, the Latin schoolboy cry and the English exclamation.

clue.text: Little boy given endless prison sentence? Gosh

indicators.note: endless means losing the last letter of the phrase just after it

blocks.note: doing time is serving a prison sentence
'My!' is an exclamation of surprise, like 'Gosh!'

explanation.surface: Shock that a small boy has been jailed for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless prison sentence' sounds like life imprisonment, but it is just TIME without its end.
explanation.definitionFit: Timmy is the pet form of Timothy, a name used for a young boy.

clue.text: Plant half strangled by nasty thorn

indicators.note: something nasty is twisted out of shape, so these letters are reordered
being strangled means being gripped all round, so one part sits inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written before being reshuffled
semi- is the prefix meaning half

explanation.surface: A gardener sees a plant half throttled by a vicious bramble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half' wants to cut a word in two; here it is the prefix for half.
explanation.definitionFit: Horsemint is a wild mint, a herb of damp ground with a strong scent.

clue.text: Beer — litres taken from bar

indicators.note: taking something from a word removes those letters from it

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for litres; this is the letter that goes
to bar is to block

explanation.surface: Litres of beer are being carried out of a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub, but it is the verb meaning obstruct.
explanation.definitionFit: Bock is a strong German lager, so it names a kind of beer.

clue.text: Fortress illuminated, as it were, in Swiss city

indicators.note: 'as it were' hints the word is not given straight, here meaning it reads the wrong way
'in' puts the illuminated word inside the name of the city

blocks.note: the English spelling of Basel
illuminated means lit

explanation.surface: A floodlit fortress stands in a city in Switzerland.
explanation.walkthrough: The turnaround signal is loose: 'as it were' must be what tells you LIT goes in backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bastille was the Paris fortress-prison stormed in 1789, and the word also means any fortress.

clue.text: Former president out east supports female as Arab leader

indicators.note: 'out east' means the compass letter for east is removed
in a down answer, what supports another piece sits underneath it

blocks.note: she is the female pronoun
Ike was the nickname of US president Eisenhower

explanation.surface: A one-time president, now in the Middle East, backs a woman as an Arab ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheik is the chief of an Arab tribe or family, an Arab leader.

clue.text: Another phone for new wing

blocks.note: first meaning: an additional telephone on the same line
second meaning: an added section built onto a house

explanation.surface: Fitting an extra telephone in a newly built part of the house.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means an addition, whether an additional telephone handset on a line or an addition built onto a building.

clue.text: Row below sandy ridge in New Zealand location

indicators.note: in a down answer, 'below' puts the row word underneath, so it comes second

blocks.note: a dune is a ridge of sand
a row is a loud noise, a din

explanation.surface: An argument breaks out below the sand hills on a New Zealand beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests a line, but it is the noise, rhyming with cow.
explanation.definitionFit: Dunedin is a city in New Zealand's South Island, founded by Scottish settlers.

clue.text: Trees in lines bordering American area

indicators.note: to border something is to sit on either side of it, so the word for lines wraps round the rest

blocks.note: railway lines are tracks
standard abbreviation for American
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A row of trees runs along the edge of some patch of land in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' here means railway lines, not rows of planting; the American area sits just after their first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tamaracks are North American larches, deciduous conifers, so the plural names a group of trees.

clue.text: Got to school, say

indicators.note: 'say' asks us to speak the school's name and hear another word in it

blocks.note: Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: Somebody simply arrived at school, perhaps late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got to' looks like 'reached', but it means bothered, as in 'what's eating you?'. Eton is England's best-known boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has got to you has upset you, and 'eaten' is used the same way for a worry gnawing at someone.

clue.text: Boisterous girl's desire to embrace boyfriend at last behind house

indicators.note: 'at last' points to the final letter of the word just before it
embracing means holding inside, so one part wraps round another
'behind' places the longer part after the shorter one in the answer

blocks.note: HO is a standard abbreviation for house
a yen is a longing
the final letter of boyfriend

explanation.surface: A rowdy girl longs to hug her boyfriend, finally, round the back of the house.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoyden is an old word for a high-spirited, unladylike girl, a tomboy.

clue.text: Disgusted ~ that's exactly right — by two little boys

indicators.note: 'by' means next to, so the boys' names follow on directly

blocks.note: Latin 'thus', put in a quotation to say it is reproduced exactly as written
two short boys' names, Ken and Ed

explanation.surface: An outraged letter-writer signs off, approving a remark made by a couple of small boys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disgusted' recalls the indignant letter-writers' signature 'Disgusted of Tunbridge Wells'. The wavy mark after it is how this copy prints a dash.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling sickened is feeling revulsion, the same state as being disgusted.

clue.text: Family sliced rolls first of all for big meal

indicators.note: something that rolls over turns round, so the word for sliced is read the other way
'first of all' puts the turned word at the front, ahead of the family word

blocks.note: sliced means cut
one's kin are one's family

explanation.surface: The family cut up bread rolls to start off a large dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolls' and 'big meal' make you think of bread, but 'rolls' is the turnaround signal and 'first of all' fixes the order of the two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A tuck-in is informal British for a hearty, filling meal, from tuck meaning food.

clue.text: Person issuing challenge against examiner

blocks.note: as in pros and cons
someone who tests

explanation.surface: A student disputes the marks and takes on the examiner.
explanation.definitionFit: One who contests something is disputing it, so a contester issues a challenge.

clue.text: Foreign lager drunk by Scotsman

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so these letters lurch into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
Ian is the stock Scottish man's name in crosswords

explanation.surface: A Scot downs a pint of imported lager.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: an Algerian is one particular kind of foreigner, so 'Foreign' defines by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Algerian describes something from Algeria, which is foreign from the British setter's point of view.

clue.text: After European proposal for debate, a Liberal's expressing feelings

indicators.note: 'After' places the debating proposal behind the European abbreviation

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
a motion is the proposal a debate argues over
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: Once a European motion is tabled, a Liberal politician gets worked up about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone emotional is openly showing their feelings, so the adjective matches the participle phrase.

clue.text: Signal failure for French railway terminal

blocks.note: first meaning: Napoleon's final, crushing defeat in 1815, a famous failure for the French
second meaning: the London mainline station of that name

explanation.surface: A signal fault has stranded passengers at a French station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Signal failure' reads as rail jargon; here 'signal' means notable. The London terminus was also where Eurostar trains from France arrived until 2007.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterloo is both the battle that ended Napoleon's rule and one of London's main railway stations, named after it.

clue.text: Edited short anecdote about a pest controller

indicators.note: something short is missing its end, so the final letter is dropped
an edited text has been reworked, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the word with its final letter removed
taken as written

explanation.surface: A short story about a person who gets rid of vermin has been cut down by an editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like the subject of the anecdote, but it just links the A to the other letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Cane toads were brought to Australia to eat beetles that attacked sugar cane, so they were meant to control pests.

clue.text: Nude appears in brief musical entertainment

indicators.note: brief means cut short, so the show's title loses its last letter
to appear in something is to be inside it, so one part sits within the other

blocks.note: the Lloyd Webber musical Cats, shortened
nude means bare

explanation.surface: A naked performer turns up in a short song-and-dance show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief musical entertainment' looks like the definition. 'Musical' is the show Cats, and only 'entertainment' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabaret is a show of songs, dancing or comedy staged in a nightclub or restaurant.

clue.text: In France, one's entertained by talented composer

indicators.note: a guest entertained by a host is taken in, so one part goes inside the other

blocks.note: good means talented
the French word for one

explanation.surface: Over in France, someone is being hosted by a gifted composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Gounod was the nineteenth-century French composer of the opera Faust.

clue.text: Salesman turned up in cart displaying collection of fabrics

indicators.note: in a down answer, turning something up flips it so it reads from bottom to top
'in' puts the salesman inside the vehicle

blocks.note: a dray is a low cart for heavy loads
a rep is a sales representative, and here it is upside down

explanation.surface: A travelling salesman arrives on a cart, showing off his bolts of cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Drapery means cloth and textiles in general, as sold by a draper.

clue.text: One's probably not dying for a rest

blocks.note: first meaning: whoever is still breathing is likely alive
second meaning: a short pause from work

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as someone not desperate for a break; the first half is really a literal coinage, one who breathes.
explanation.definitionFit: A breather is a brief break to recover, and in a jokey literal sense anyone who breathes.

clue.text: I wouldn't put up paintings

indicators.note: in a down answer, putting something up turns it to read from bottom to top

blocks.note: 'I wouldn't' can be said 'I'd not'

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to hang a set of pictures on the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up paintings' reads like hanging pictures, but 'put up' turns the words before it upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A tondo is a circular painting or relief, and tondi is its Italian plural.

clue.text: Feature of busiest afternoons? Yes and no

definitions.text: Feature of busiest afternoons? Yes and no

indicators.note: a feature is part of something, so the letters sit inside the next words

blocks.note: the run of letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A puzzle about what typifies the most hectic part of the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yes and no' admits the joke: the word is a feature of the letters 'busiest afternoons', yet an afternoon nap is never part of a busy one.
explanation.definitionFit: A siesta is the afternoon nap of hot countries, a regular feature of the afternoon but not of a hectic one.

clue.text: Some Klosters inhabitants enjoy recreation — primarily this one?

definitions.text: Some Klosters inhabitants enjoy recreation — primarily this one?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each word is used

blocks.note: the opening letters of these five words

explanation.surface: Visitors to a Swiss ski resort have fun, mostly on the slopes.
explanation.walkthrough: Klosters is a Swiss ski resort, so the whole clue describes the answer too: its residents mostly unwind on skis.
explanation.definitionFit: Klosters is an Alpine winter-sports resort, so the typical person there enjoying leisure is someone on skis.

clue.text: Travel over vast, endless desert

indicators.note: endless means losing the last letter of the word just before it
in a down answer, 'over' places the travel word above the other piece

blocks.note: to go is to travel
vast means big

explanation.surface: A journey crosses an enormous, seemingly unending desert.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gobi is the great desert spanning Mongolia and northern China.

clue.text: What can provide dietary supplement? Half portion of rusk can

indicators.note: half a portion means only the front half of the following word is used

blocks.note: the first two of its four letters
a can is a tin

explanation.surface: Half a baby's rusk out of a tin is offered as a health supplement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb, but it is the container, a tin.
explanation.definitionFit: Rutin is a plant flavonoid sold in capsules as a nutritional supplement.

clue.text: Snail one mixed with unknown ingredient and cooked with onions

indicators.note: mixing stirs things together, so these letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
y is an algebraic unknown, here one more ingredient of the mix

explanation.surface: A recipe: a snail is mixed with a mystery ingredient and fried with onions.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen surface hides that 'unknown' is the letter used for an unknown in algebra.
explanation.definitionFit: Lyonnaise describes food prepared in the style of Lyon, which means with sliced fried onions.

clue.text: Briefly thanks these volunteers

blocks.note: surface reading: a curt word of gratitude to some helpers
setter's reading: the short British word of thanks is also the initials of a reserve force of part-time soldiers

explanation.surface: Someone gives a quick thank-you to a group of helpers.
explanation.walkthrough: Ta is British slang for thanks, and TA is also the standard abbreviation of the volunteers in question, the UK's part-time army reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: The Territorial Army was Britain's force of volunteer reservist soldiers, now called the Army Reserve.
